nameStory: The 'harlequin' in rock harlequin comes from the plant's delightfully colorful flowers that mix pink, yellow, and white like a jester's costume. The 'rock' part hints at where you'll find this charming wildflower - scrambling over rocky outcrops and stone-filled woodland clearings throughout New England.
description: Rock harlequin is a delicate annual or biennial wildflower that brings splashes of pink and yellow to rocky places. This graceful plant grows 1-4 feet tall with finely divided, blue-green leaves that look almost fern-like. Its most striking feature is clusters of tubular flowers that bloom in shades of pink with bright yellow tips, creating a two-toned effect that's unmistakable once you've seen it. The plant has a somewhat sprawling habit, often growing in loose colonies across disturbed or rocky ground.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular flowers about half an inch long with pink petals tipped in bright yellow, arranged in loose clusters at stem tips. Each flower has a distinctive spurred shape and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided blue-green leaves that feel smooth and somewhat waxy, divided into many small segments that give them a delicate, almost feathery appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems that often sprawl or lean, creating loose patches rather than standing rigidly upright.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops narrow, elongated seed pods that split open when ripe, releasing small black seeds that have a slightly rough texture.

habitat: Look for rock harlequin in rocky woodlands, stone walls, talus slopes, and areas that have been recently disturbed by fire or clearing. It thrives in partially shaded spots with well-drained, often thin soils where competition from other plants is reduced. You'll often find it growing in the cracks and crevices of rock outcrops or along rocky stream banks.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early with their distinctive blue-green foliage beginning to develop. Late spring brings the first flower buds forming at stem tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the showy pink and yellow flowers are most abundant and easiest to spot. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods mature, splitting open to release seeds. Plants begin to yellow and die back if they're annuals.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, while biennial plants may persist as small rosettes of leaves close to the ground, though these are hard to spot.

funFact: Rock harlequin is actually a fire-follower - its seeds can lie dormant in the soil for years until a forest fire or major disturbance creates the perfect conditions for them to sprout, suddenly carpeting burned areas with their cheerful pink and yellow blooms.
confusionNotes: The finely divided leaves might be confused with wild bleeding heart, but rock harlequin's flowers are distinctly two-toned pink and yellow rather than solid pink or white. Remember: harlequin has two colors like a jester's outfit, bleeding heart is usually just one color.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly placed in the genus Corydalis and you may still see it listed as Corydalis sempervirens in older field guides. It's now recognized as the sole member of its own genus Capnoides, making it quite special among New England wildflowers.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Capnoides in our region, rock harlequin is most similar to other members of the poppy family like Corydalis species. However, rock harlequin's distinctive pink-and-yellow two-toned flowers and preference for rocky, disturbed sites sets it apart from the more uniformly colored flowers of true Corydalis species. The blue-green, finely divided foliage is also more delicate-looking than most of its poppy family relatives.
